solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Endless optimism in Hunt’s business discussion (4,4)

indicatorNotes.Endless: a word with no end has lost its last letter, so HOPE becomes HOP
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the shortened word inside the next one, so HOP sits within STALK

blocks.note: to stalk = to hunt; the outer letters S…TALK
HOPE without its last letter, placed inside STALK

annotation.surface: Someone in a meeting with a man called Hunt, full of relentless optimism about the business.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hunt’s' looks like a person’s name in the possessive, as if a politician called Hunt were talking business; it is the verb, stalks.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: talking shop means chatting about work matters.

entries.clue: Hôtel Ritz initially full of rage for customer paying by the hour? (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: 'initially' means at the start, so take the first letter of each word
indicatorNotes.full of: the two letters are full of the next word, which fills the gap between them

blocks.note: first letters of Hôtel and Ritz, H…R
ire = rage, placed between H and R

annotation.surface: A guest storming through a grand Paris hotel in a fury.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: someone hiring a car or a room is charged by time.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: someone renting a car or boat is often charged per hour.

entries.clue: Is plum hat wrong for snappy dresser (a 5 13)? (4,5)

indicatorNotes.wrong: the letters as given are wrong, so they must be put into the right order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A fashion critic declaring that a plum-coloured hat is a mistake for a sharp dresser.
annotation.walkthrough: Paul Smith is a British fashion designer; the bracket points to 5 down (KENWOOD, where the FT Weekend Festival is held), marking him as one of the festival’s speakers.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the designer is known for sharp tailoring, so snappy works for him and his clothes.

entries.clue: Disliking history, love part of Italian course (9)

blocks.note: anti = against, disliking
history = the past
love = nil = O, as in tennis

annotation.surface: A student who hates history but loves one part of an Italian course of study.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Italian course' reads as a language class; the course is the run of dishes at dinner, and the starter is one part of it.
annotation.definitionFit: The antipasto is the starter of an Italian meal, one stage of its sequence of dishes.

entries.clue: King to stop holding court in London house (7)

indicatorNotes.holding: one word holds another in its arms, so END takes WOO inside

blocks.note: K = king, in chess and cards
to end = to stop
to court = to woo, placed inside END as EN…D

annotation.surface: A monarch halting proceedings while holding court in a London mansion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Court' sits beside 'King' as a royal court; it is the verb, to woo. Kenwood House is a stately home on Hampstead Heath, home of the FT Weekend Festival.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Kenwood House is a stately home on Hampstead Heath.

entries.clue: Minister first on list PM sent round in shake-up (6)

indicatorNotes.sent round: something sent round turns to face the other way, so PM reads MP

blocks.note: a minister of religion is a Reverend, REV
A is the label of a list’s first item
PM turned round

annotation.surface: A prime minister reshuffling the cabinet and putting a minister at the top of the list.
annotation.walkthrough: The political surface points 'Minister' at government; it is a clergyman, and the PM is only there to be turned into an MP.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an overhaul or reorganisation of something.

entries.clue: Villain shot from behind in Parisian street (5)

indicatorNotes.from behind: read from behind means starting at the back, so GO becomes OG
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the reversed word inside the street

blocks.note: rue is French for street; the outer letters R…UE
a shot = a go, read backwards, inside RUE

annotation.surface: A gangster gunned down in the back on a street in Paris.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shot' reads as gunfire in the crime scene; it is a noun, an attempt, a go.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a scoundrel, a dishonest rascal.

entries.clue: Choosing resident doctor or vet? (5)

indicatorNotes.doctor: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A trainee deciding between becoming a resident doctor or a vet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resident doctor' reads as a hospital post; the phrase splits, and 'doctor' is the instruction applied to OR VET.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: an elector is someone living in a place who picks a candidate at the polls.

entries.clue: Madonna and Shakespeare gone into by English academic (a 5 13) (4,5)

indicatorNotes.gone into by: BARD is entered by the letter E, which goes inside it

blocks.note: the Madonna is the Virgin Mary
Shakespeare is the Bard; the outer letters B…ARD
E = English, going into BARD

annotation.surface: A pop star and a playwright being studied by an English academic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Madonna' looks like the singer; it is the Virgin Mary. The bracket marks the classicist as a speaker at the festival at 5 down.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: she is a Cambridge classics professor and broadcaster.

entries.clue: Writer for the FT back from toilet… (6)

indicatorNotes.back from: the back of a word is its end, so take the final letter of toilet

blocks.note: pro = for, in favour of
the setter writes for the FT, so the FT is 'us'
the last letter of toileT

annotation.surface: A newspaper columnist just returned from the loo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer for the FT' looks like the definition; only 'Writer' is. The ellipsis runs this lavatory scene on into 10 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Marcel Proust was the French novelist of In Search of Lost Time.

entries.clue: …piddling with an arm around Michael Gove? (8)

indicatorNotes.around: turned around means facing the other way, so A GUN reads NUGA

blocks.note: an arm = A GUN, turned round
Michael Gove is a Conservative (Tory) politician; the question mark says he is an example

annotation.surface: Continuing from 9 across, someone relieving themselves while putting an arm round a politician.
annotation.walkthrough: After the toilet in 9 across, 'piddling' looks like more of the same; here it means trivial. Tory is the nickname for the UK Conservative party.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: of no value or importance, trifling.

entries.clue: Assume winning attitude keeps president ahead (10)

indicatorNotes.keeps: the phrase keeps another piece with it, so PRES is added on
indicatorNotes.ahead: ahead means in front, so PRES goes at the start

blocks.note: Pres. is the abbreviation of president
up = ahead, winning, as in 'two goals up'
a pose = an attitude, a stance

annotation.surface: A candidate taking on a winner’s swagger while keeping the president in front.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue lists the pieces in the wrong order, and 'keeps president ahead' is what moves the president to the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to take something for granted in advance.

entries.clue: Unsophisticated American back to front in taxi (4)

indicatorNotes.back to front: the back letter is sent to the front, so UBER's final R leads

blocks.note: Uber, the ride-hailing firm, stands for a taxi; its back letter R goes first
the rest of UBER follows

annotation.surface: A naive American tourist sitting the wrong way round in a cab.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' wants to reverse the whole word, giving REBU; only the back letter goes to the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: US slang for a naive country bumpkin.

entries.clue: One cuts a lot of meat for fishing bait (5)

indicatorNotes.cuts: the letter cuts into the word, splitting it in two
indicatorNotes.a lot of: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so FLESH loses its last letter

blocks.note: FLESH without its last letter; the outer letters FL…ES
I = one, the Roman numeral, cutting into FLES

annotation.surface: A butcher slicing up a quantity of meat to use as bait for fishing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One cuts' reads as a butcher at work; 'One' is the letter I.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: anglers dangle real or artificial insects to hook fish.

entries.clue: Actor (a 5 13) neglected child climbing around on smoking waste (5,4)

indicatorNotes.climbing: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so WAIF becomes FIAW
indicatorNotes.around: the reversed word goes around the others, holding them inside

blocks.note: a waif is a neglected child; WAIF read upwards, the outer letters FI…AW
on is used as itself, inside FIAW
ash is what smoking leaves, inside FIAW after ON

annotation.surface: A child actor left alone, scrambling about on a heap of smouldering rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: The bracket marks her as a speaker at the festival at 5 down.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Irish performer is known for stage work and Killing Eve.

entries.clue: For this US politician, pitch humour mostly to the left (8)

indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means not quite all, so COMEDY loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.to the left: in an across entry, going to the left means reading right to left

blocks.note: pitch = tar, the black sticky stuff
COMEDY without its last letter
TAR COMED read from right to left

annotation.surface: A campaign adviser urging a politician to slant their jokes leftwards.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pitches humour to the left as politics; 'to the left' is the reading direction, and 'pitch' is the substance, tar.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a member of the Democratic Party, the more left-leaning of the two big US parties.

entries.clue: Techy university admitting additional women is common sense (6,3)

indicatorNotes.admitting: a university admitting students lets them in, so MIT lets OTHER and W inside

blocks.note: MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology; the outer letters M…IT
other = additional, inside MIT
W = women, inside MIT after OTHER

annotation.surface: A news story about a technical university finally letting in more women students.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a debate about admissions, with 'common sense' its verdict.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: native good judgement, the practical wit one is born with.

entries.clue: Unit possibly connected to 5 18s in Escort, ear splitting (3,6)

indicatorNotes.splitting: the words are split apart and their letters remade into new words

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A deafening sound system blaring inside a Ford Escort.
annotation.walkthrough: 5 and 18 down give KENWOOD SPEAKERS; Kenwood is also a brand of car audio. The Escort is a Ford car, fitting the definition as well as the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an in-car sound system could well be wired to Kenwood-brand speakers.

entries.clue: Male youths repelled lout and thugs (8)

indicatorNotes.repelled: something repelled is driven back, so YOB is read backwards

blocks.note: a lout = a yob, turned back
hoods = hoodlums, thugs

annotation.surface: Young men fending off a lout and his gang.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Male youths' reads as young men; it means the times of being young, as in 'their boyhoods'. YOB is British slang for a lout.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the abstract sense of youth: the years of being a young lad.

entries.clue: Ask peer specially for senior Parliamentary role (7)

indicatorNotes.specially: something made specially is reworked for a purpose, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Advice to seek out a member of the House of Lords for a senior post.
annotation.walkthrough: A peer is a member of the House of Lords, which makes the surface plausible.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the presiding officer who chairs debates in the House of Commons.

entries.clue: Stale wine on trip in odd places (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A on B puts A after B, so the wine follows
indicatorNotes.in odd places: take the letters in the odd-numbered places of the word

blocks.note: TrIp, letters 1 and 3
red = red wine

annotation.surface: Flat wine served on a journey through strange places.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Odd places' sounds like strange destinations on the trip; it means odd-numbered positions.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: overused and lacking freshness, as with an old joke.

entries.clue: Possible route for mountaineer secured by sherpa’s sweat (4)

indicatorNotes.secured by: the answer is held securely inside the words that follow

blocks.note: sherPA’S Sweat

annotation.surface: A climber roped up, relying on the sweat of the local guide.
annotation.walkthrough: Sherpas are the Himalayan people famed as mountain guides, which is why they sit so naturally here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gap or col through a mountain range that climbers can cross.

entries.clue: Seductress touching wrong trousers (5)

indicatorNotes.trousers: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so it takes something inside

blocks.note: a sin = a wrong; the outer letters SI…N
re = concerning, touching on, inside SIN

annotation.surface: A femme fatale fingering the wrong pair of trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing in this racy scene; it is a verb, pockets. To trouser is British slang for pocketing money.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, after the Sirens of Greek myth who lured sailors to their doom.

entries.clue: 5 for the FT festival, the place to be? (5,3,2)

blocks.note: 5 down, KENWOOD, is literally where the FT Weekend Festival is held
the idiom for somewhere fashionable

annotation.surface: A plug for the newspaper’s own festival as the fashionable place to be.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense takes the phrase literally: Kenwood (5 down) is where the festival is at.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for the most fashionable spot, and also literally the venue of the festival.

entries.clue: Any people that work sound really happy (5)

blocks.note: who = whichever people, as in 'who wants one'
op. = opus, a work

annotation.surface: Anyone with a job ought to be cheerful.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' looks like employment in the surface; it is a musical work, an opus.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to let out a loud cry of joy.

entries.clue: Everybody agreed to calm down (5)

blocks.note: all = everybody
ay (aye) = yes, agreed

annotation.surface: A meeting voting unanimously to settle down.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence, everybody agreeing to calm down; 'to' is only the link.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to soothe or relieve fears or anger.

entries.clue: Eye buffet sandwiches that woman’s left (8)

indicatorNotes.sandwiches: to sandwich is to hold filling between two halves, so SOCK wraps round HER and L

blocks.note: to buffet = to hit, sock; the outer letters S…OCK
her = that woman’s, inside SOCK
L = left, inside SOCK after HER

annotation.surface: Someone who has left behind the sandwiches from a buffet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' and 'sandwiches' paint a party spread; buffet is the verb, to strike, and sandwiches is a verb too. A private eye is a detective.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: eye is slang for a private detective, and Holmes is the most famous.

entries.clue: Fun with this game could be wonderful (6)

indicatorNotes.could be: the letters could be turned into the other word, so the two are anagrams of each other

blocks.note: WONDERFUL with the letters of FUN taken out
the letters removed from WONDERFUL
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A cheerful endorsement of a game that is great fun.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: FUN plus the answer could be rearranged into WONDERFUL, so the answer is what is left of WONDERFUL once FUN is removed, reordered.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the daily online five-letter guessing puzzle.

entries.clue: Blithely arrive weak through drink (4,2)

indicatorNotes.through: one word runs through the middle of the other, so WAN splits SUP

blocks.note: to sup = to drink; the outer letters S…UP
wan = pale and weak, inside SUP

annotation.surface: Someone breezing in, the worse for drink.
annotation.walkthrough: To swan is British for moving about in a casual, carefree way.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to turn up casually, without a care.

entries.clue: Name changed to suit new circumstances confused Terry — no, Mike (8)

annotation.definition: Name changed to suit new circumstances

indicatorNotes.confused: a confused name has been muddled, so the letters of TERRY NO M need sorting out

blocks.note: anagram fodder
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet, joining the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone muddled over whether a man is Terry or Mike, his name having been changed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a mix-up over a man’s name; the answer names a new term for an old thing, like 'acoustic guitar' once electric ones arrived.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain gloss: a term coined for an original thing once a newer version exists.
